note: Non-temporal economics: macroeconomic concepts (classical/Keynesian frameworks, aggregate demand/supply, circular flow, economy types). Awaiting future non-temporal economics architecture.

nodes.label: Emergence of Macroeconomics
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Macroeconomics emerged as a separate branch after the Great Depression of the 1930s. John Maynard Keynes' 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' (1936) showed that markets may not self-correct and government intervention may be needed. Before Keynes, classical economists believed markets always clear.

nodes.label: Keynesian Economics
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Economic theory developed by J.M. Keynes arguing that aggregate demand determines the level of economic activity. In a depression, market forces alone cannot restore full employment; government must increase expenditure to boost demand. Advocates active fiscal policy -- deficit spending during recessions.

nodes.label: Aggregate Demand
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The total demand for final goods and services in an economy at a given time. Components: Consumption (C), Investment (I), Government Expenditure (G), and Net Exports (X-M). In a closed economy: AD = C + I + G. In an open economy: AD = C + I + G + (X-M).

nodes.label: Aggregate Supply
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The total supply of goods and services produced in an economy during a specific period at a given price level. In Keynesian analysis of the short run, aggregate supply is assumed to be perfectly elastic up to the full employment level, and prices are sticky.

nodes.label: Four Sectors of an Economy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Macroeconomics models the economy with four sectors: (1) Households -- consume goods and supply factors, (2) Firms -- produce goods and hire factors, (3) Government -- taxes, spends, and regulates, (4) External sector -- foreign trade and capital flows. A two-sector model has only households and firms.

nodes.label: Circular Flow of Income
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The continuous flow of income and expenditure between different sectors of the economy. Households provide factors to firms and receive factor income. They spend this income on goods from firms. Injections (investment, govt spending, exports) add to the flow; leakages (savings, taxes, imports) withdraw from it.

nodes.label: Classical Economics
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Pre-Keynesian economic thought (Adam Smith, Ricardo, J.B. Say) that believed free markets automatically achieve full employment. Say's Law states 'supply creates its own demand'. Wages and prices are assumed to be flexible, ensuring markets clear. The Great Depression challenged these beliefs.

nodes.label: Open Economy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: An economy that interacts with the rest of the world through trade in goods, services, and financial assets. National income in an open economy: Y = C + I + G + (X - M). Most modern economies are open economies with varying degrees of openness.

nodes.label: Closed Economy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: An economy that has no economic interactions with the rest of the world -- no imports, exports, or capital flows. National income: Y = C + I + G. A purely closed economy is theoretical; no real-world economy is completely closed.

nodes.label: Injections and Leakages
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Injections add to the circular flow of income: investment (I), government expenditure (G), and exports (X). Leakages withdraw from the flow: savings (S), taxes (T), and imports (M). Equilibrium requires total injections to equal total leakages: I + G + X = S + T + M.

nodes.label: Economic Growth
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Sustained increase in real GDP or per capita real income over time. Measured by the growth rate of real GDP. Usually coupled with inflation. Capital formation is necessary for economic growth. Per capita real income is the most appropriate measure of a country's economic growth.
